answer: Because whenever processes must coordinate to keep data consistent (e.g. two distributed transactions updating the same row, where one must stop the other), you need a lock they all respect, and in a distributed setup there is no single database to lean on. So remote and distributed locks form the heart and crux of data correctness and consistency.
evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'Imagine two transactions running in a distributed fashion, both trying to update the same row... they form the heart and crux of data correctness and consistency.'

answer: Multiple components on multiple machines that form a single coherent system which solves a bigger problem. answer: Yes, two clients can both believe they hold it: after two of C1's nodes crash and restart empty, C2 can lock them plus a free node, three of five. As taught it is minimized because losers keep failing to get more than 50% and release, while C1 keeps acquiring the remaining nodes so the system converges to C1 holding all; the edge case needs both nodes to go down in the 2-3 seconds before C1 grabs the rest, so the probability is very low. More precisely the window is the whole TTL; Redis fixes it with delayed restarts (keep a crashed node out longer than the max TTL) or AOF fsync=always. Another option: a global state saying the cluster is unhealthy, wait for two more nodes.
evidence: Ch7 §7.3 'The edge case', the two arguments, and the More precisely note.
